opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underappreciated questions when people forecast how quickly AI will transform the economy. There's a tendency to look at benchmark results, see a system doing very well on some test of coding or reasoning, and conclude that it can just slot in and do the work of a senior engineer or analyst. But when you think about what actually makes a senior person valuable inside an organisation, a lot of it isn't raw capability. It's context.

Think about a very talented person who joins a new company. Even if they're brilliant, they typically aren't operating at full senior effectiveness on day one. It might take them months, sometimes a year or more, to learn the codebase, the history of why certain decisions were made, who to ask about what, which projects are politically sensitive, what the customers actually care about, and all the tacit knowledge that never got written down. A huge amount of senior-level judgement is really just accumulated familiarity with a particular environment.

So the question for AI is: how long does that onboarding take for a system? And there are reasons to think it could go either way. On one hand, an AI can read every document, every Slack thread, every commit message in a fraction of the time a human could. That's a real advantage. On the other hand, a lot of the crucial knowledge isn't in those artefacts at all. It's in people's heads, or it's implicit in how things are done. And current systems also have real limitations around memory and learning over long horizons. They often don't retain and build on what they've learned the way a person does across weeks and months, unless that's been carefully engineered around.

There's also a connection to the work on task length, the observation that the length of tasks AI agents can reliably complete has been growing roughly exponentially. Senior work tends to involve very long-horizon tasks, projects that unfold over weeks or months, with lots of ambiguity and changing goals. So even if the trend continues, you have to ask how far along that curve we need to be before a system can operate at that level, and then add on top of that whatever the effective onboarding time is.

My overall view is that this is a source of friction that will slow things down somewhat relative to naive forecasts, but I wouldn't lean on it too heavily as a reason for comfort. If systems get good at continual learning, that onboarding period could shrink dramatically, and once one instance has learned the context, you can potentially copy it. That's something you simply can't do with a human employee. So it might look like a significant bottleneck right up until the point where it isn't, and then the change could be quite abrupt.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI onboarding time but gives no estimate ranging from roughly six months to 20 years across jobs. The months-to-a-year example is about a human joining a company.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn as Toby Ord, drawing only on the conversation given.

Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated aspects of the whole picture. When people imagine an AI system that can do the work of, say, a senior researcher or a senior engineer, they tend to picture something you switch on and it's immediately operating at that level. But if you look at how humans actually reach senior performance in an organisation, a huge amount of it isn't raw ability. It's accumulated context. It's knowing who to ask, what the unwritten norms are, which projects were tried before and why they failed, what the actual priorities are as opposed to the stated ones. A brilliant person who walks in the door on day one is genuinely not performing at a senior level on day one, even if they have all the underlying skills. It usually takes months, sometimes years, to get there.

So the interesting question is how much of that transfers to AI, and in which direction. On one hand, an AI might absorb that context much faster. It could read every document the company has ever produced in an afternoon, which no human can do. So some of the onboarding time might collapse dramatically. On the other hand, a lot of that institutional knowledge isn't written down anywhere. It lives in people's heads, in conversations, in the way decisions actually get made. And there's a question of whether an AI gets access to that at all, and whether it's trusted enough to be given the kind of responsibility where it could learn from making real decisions.

I think that matters for timelines in a way that often gets skipped over. Even if the underlying capability arrives on a particular date, there's a lag between "could in principle do senior work" and "is actually doing senior work across the economy", and part of that lag is just this ramp-up period for each deployment. Now, the counterargument is that once one instance has learned something, you can copy it, so the ramp-up only needs to happen once per organisation rather than once per worker. That's a real asymmetry with humans, and it could make the transition much more abrupt than the human analogy suggests. But I don't think it makes the lag zero. There's still that first period of getting embedded, building trust, being given access, and that's bounded by human and organisational speed, not just by the AI's speed.

So when I think about it, I try to hold both of those in mind. The human analogy says "expect a meaningful delay"; the copying argument says "but maybe much less than you'd naively think, and then very fast afterwards". I'd be suspicious of anyone who was confident about which of those dominates.

r001.rationale: The response says onboarding to senior performance can take “months, sometimes years,” but it does not give the roughly six-month-to-20-year range across different jobs.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between having the capabilities needed to do the job and having the context needed to do it well. Even a very capable person joining a company needs time to understand how things work: what people have tried, why certain decisions were made, and who knows what. At a senior level, that context can be a substantial part of the job.

An AI might be able to acquire some of that much faster, by reading through documents and correspondence. But some of it may only emerge through working with people, asking questions, and seeing how decisions play out. So I wouldn’t assume that being capable of senior-level work means being able to arrive and perform at that level immediately. The key question is how much of that settling-in period can be compressed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses onboarding context and says the settling-in period may be compressed, but it gives no estimate or range of roughly six months to 20 years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between having the capabilities to do the job and having the context to do it well. If you hired a very capable person into a senior role, you wouldn’t expect them to be fully effective on their first day. They need to understand what the company is trying to achieve, why certain decisions were made, and who knows what.

An AI might be able to read the company’s documents much faster than a person could. But some of that context won’t be written down, and some of it may only become apparent through doing the work and seeing what happens. So I wouldn’t assume that being sufficiently intelligent means it can immediately perform at a senior level. There could still be a period of learning about that particular organisation. How long that takes seems like an important uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response says there could be a period of learning and that its duration is uncertain, but it does not estimate a range of roughly six months to 20 years across different jobs.
